transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, Doctor, I honestly wasn't sure about coming in today, but I knew I had to do something because things at work are just... they're really falling apart, honestly. I've been a quality inspector for a long time, and I've always prided myself on being professional, you know, making sure the samples are tested right and the weights are exact. It's a job that takes focus and a level head. But lately, I just... I’m here because I keep snapping at people. 

It's like I have absolutely zero patience anymore, just this very short fuse. For example, just the other day, we were all sitting in this big mandatory safety meeting, and one of the shift managers was going over some routine stuff about the sorting line, and I don't even know what set me off exactly, but I just started yelling. I was practically screaming across the room before I could even stop myself. It was like a switch flipped and I couldn't pull it back, my heart was just pounding and the words were flying out. It was awful, and embarrassing, really, to lose it like that in front of the whole floor. 

And the worst part is the aftermath. Now all the younger inspectors—the new kids they just hired out of high school—they act completely scared to even look at me, let alone ask me anything. They’ll probably make a mistake on a sample batch rather than come ask me for help because they think I'm going to bite their heads off. I can see it in their eyes, they're terrified of me. And I hate that, I really do, because I'm not a cruel person, but I just can't seem to stop this anger from boiling over, and I just keep replaying that meeting in my head and how everyone stared at me...
Is this irritability and quickness to anger something that only happens at work, or do you find yourself getting easily upset in other parts of your life too, like at home or with friends?

No, it's... it's definitely not just at work. I wish it was, I really do, because then maybe I could just, you know, leave it at the door when I clock out. But it follows me home. It's everywhere. Like, just last weekend, my husband, Jim, he was just trying to help out around the house, which he does, he's a good man. He was unloading the dishwasher, and he put the good coffee mugs—the ones my sister got us for our anniversary, the heavy ceramic ones—he put them on the top shelf where the water glasses usually go. And I don't know why, but seeing them there, it just... it infuriated me. I mean, completely set me off. 

I started yelling at him about how he never pays attention, how he's always messing up my system in the kitchen, just really laying into him over coffee mugs. And he just stood there, holding a spatula, looking at me like I was a stranger. And the look on his face, it was just like the new kids at work—just this total shock and, and fear, honestly. And then I felt terrible, just this heavy, awful guilt in my chest, but in the moment, the anger was so hot and so fast I couldn't swallow it down. 

And it's not just Jim, either. I went to the grocery store on Tuesday, just a quick trip for milk and bread, and the woman in front of me in the checkout line was taking forever, counting out exact change, pennies and dimes, and chatting with the cashier about her garden. Normally, I wouldn't care. I'd just read a magazine or look at my phone. But I could feel my jaw clenching, and my hands were shaking, and I actually muttered under my breath, "Hurry up, some of us have lives," loud enough for her to hear. She turned around and glared at me, and I just... I felt so ugly inside. I'm alienating my husband, I'm snapping at strangers in the checkout line, I'm terrifying my coworkers... it's like I'm just this walking ball of rage and I don't even know who I am anymore. It's exhausting, Doctor, it really is, just being so angry all the time and not being able to stop it.
Doctor: Have you noticed feeling down, sad, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy, like hobbies or time with family?

No, not really. I mean, I wouldn't say I feel sad, like crying in bed kind of sad, you know? It's not like that. And I still do the things I normally do, like I still go to work every day, I still keep the house clean, I still make dinner for Jim. I haven't stopped doing any of that. But I guess... well, I don't know if this is what you mean, but I just don't have the patience for anything anymore. 

Like, my sister, she loves to come over on Sundays and do these big puzzle boards with me. We used to sit there for hours, drinking tea and finding the edge pieces, just chatting about the neighbors or whatever. It was nice. But the last few times she came over, I just couldn't sit still. I'd sit down, look at all those little pieces scattered everywhere, and I'd just feel this... this tightness in my chest. I'd start getting agitated, thinking about how long it was going to take, and how the pieces weren't fitting together fast enough. I actually had to get up and start vacuuming the living room right in the middle of it because I just couldn't stand sitting there. She looked so confused, asking me if she did something wrong, and I just told her I had chores to do. 

So it's not that I've lost interest in the puzzle itself, or that I don't want to spend time with my sister—I love my sister, I really do—it's just that I can't handle the... the sitting, the waiting, the focus it takes. My brain is just going a million miles an hour and I just feel so on edge all the time. It's like I don't have the bandwidth for anything that isn't absolutely necessary. But sad? No, I wouldn't use the word sad. Just angry. And tired. So very tired of being angry.
Do you find yourself feeling anxious, worried, or on edge most days, even when there isn’t a specific reason for it?

Well, "on edge" is... I mean, that's almost putting it lightly, Doctor. It’s like I’m constantly waiting for the other shoe to drop, even when I know perfectly well there are no shoes, if that makes sense. It’s this intense physical thing, this constant buzzing in my nerves. 

Like, okay, take the break room at work. You’re supposed to go in there, sit down, maybe get a stale coffee from the machine, and just turn your brain off for fifteen minutes, right? Just a normal break. But I can’t do it. I go in there, and I absolutely have to sit at the table facing the hallway. I’m just sitting there, completely tense, watching the doors. Every single time the door swings open, my heart skips a beat. And I’m constantly straining my ears, listening for sudden machine noises from the sorting floor, even though the walls are supposed to be somewhat soundproofed. If a conveyor belt clanks too loudly or a forklift backs up and drops a pallet, I practically jump out of my skin. 

And it’s not just at the plant, either, which is the crazy part. I go to choir rehearsal on Thursday nights—I’ve been singing alto with this community group for, gosh, almost ten years now, in the exact same basement room at the rec center. Same people, same piano, it should be the safest place in the world. But lately, I can’t even focus on the sheet music. If I don't get a seat in the very back row, right up against the cinderblock wall, I am a total wreck. I spend the whole two hours just... checking who’s moving behind me, turning my head if someone shifts their weight in their folding chair or gets up to use the restroom. The director, Susan, she actually stopped rehearsal last week to ask if I was looking for someone because I kept craning my neck around to stare at the sopranos behind me. I had to make up some silly excuse about a stiff neck. 

But the truth is, no matter where I am or how logical I try to be about the situation, it's like... it's like my body just won't believe I'm safe. My logical mind knows I'm just drinking coffee or singing a hymn, but my body is locked in this state of absolute panic, treating every sound and every movement like a deadly threat. It’s just so exhausting, constantly guarding myself against nothing at all, all day, every day.
Have you gone through any particularly stressful or traumatic experiences recently, or even in the past, that you feel might be connected to how you're feeling now?

Well, yes. I mean, I know exactly what started all this. It’s not a mystery to me, Doctor. It’s... well, it was the accident at the plant. I work as a quality inspector on the sorting line, have for a long time, and we always, always worked the day shift. My body was used to it. Jim and I had our routine. But then management, in their infinite wisdom, decided they needed to increase production to meet some new corporate quota, so they implemented this massive overnight schedule change. Just completely flipped our hours upside down with barely a week's notice. 

It was awful. Everyone was just exhausted, walking around like zombies, drinking that terrible breakroom coffee trying to keep our eyes open under those buzzing fluorescent lights. People were making mistakes, dropping things, just dragging. And then... it was a Tuesday night, or I guess Wednesday morning, technically, around 3 AM. There was a... a horrible machinery accident on the main floor. 

I don't even like closing my eyes and picturing it because it just makes my chest seize up all over again, but a piece of the heavy sorting equipment just catastrophically malfunctioned. The noise, Doctor, it was deafening—just this awful, violent grinding and the sound of screaming metal, and then people were shouting, and the emergency alarms were going off. It was absolute chaos. People were running, and you didn't know who was hurt or what was going to collapse next. 

And ever since that night... well, that's when all this started. The anger, the jumping at every little clank or bang, the having to sit with my back against the cinderblock wall at choir practice. This whole nightmare has been going on since that machinery accident after the overnight schedule change. I've been keeping track, and it's been about two years and four months now. Two years and four months of just... jumping out of my skin and snapping at poor Jim because my brain is still stuck on that factory floor in the middle of the night. I just keep thinking, you know, if they hadn't changed our schedule, if we hadn't all been so dead tired, maybe someone would have caught the machine fault earlier before it broke apart. But they didn't. And now I'm just... I'm stuck like this, two years and four months later, and I just can't seem to turn it off.
